sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What problem does a CDN solve, and when would you NOT use one?
**Answer:** A CDN reduces latency for users geographically far from your origin, offloads bandwidth and TLS handshake cost from your origin, and absorbs traffic spikes by serving from cache. The fundamental mechanism is edge caching: instead of every user fetching bytes from your origin (which may be 200 ms away), users fetch from a nearby edge PoP (5 ms away). Akamai delivers ~30% of internet traffic this way. You would NOT use a CDN when: (1) your content is highly dynamic and per-user (e.g., a personalized feed where every response differs — caching provides little benefit), though edge compute can help here; (2) your traffic is all from one region and your origin is already there (the CDN adds a hop without saving latency); (3) your content is subject to legal restrictions that forbid caching outside specific jurisdictions (e.g., HIPAA medical data, GDPR-sensitive EU data); (4) your traffic is too low to justify the operational complexity or minimum spend; (5) you need strong consistency guarantees that CDN caching makes hard — a single global database write that must be visible everywhere immediately is a poor fit for a multi-region CDN edge layer.
**Visual:**
```
Without CDN:                      With CDN:
  user Tokyo -> origin US-East      user Tokyo -> Tokyo edge -> (miss) -> origin
  200ms latency + origin load       5ms on hit, 200ms on miss (cached for TTL)
                                    origin load drops 10-100x
                                    TLS terminated at edge (CPU savings)
```

### Q2. Explain origin pull vs origin push. When is each appropriate?
**Answer:** Origin pull is the default for web CDNs: the edge fetches content from origin on first request, caches it, and serves subsequent requests from cache until TTL expires. It is lazy — only content users actually request gets cached. This is appropriate for web assets (JS, CSS, images), API responses that are cacheable, and long-tail content where you cannot predict demand. Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront all use origin pull by default. Origin push is the opposite: the origin proactively uploads content to edges in advance of demand. This is appropriate when you have massive concurrent demand that would melt the origin — Netflix Open Connect pre-positions new episode encodes onto ISP-resident appliances hours before release, so when 10 million people hit "play" simultaneously the bytes are already local and the origin never sees the spike. Origin push requires the CDN to predict demand (a Netflix new-release schedule), while origin pull adapts automatically but cannot absorb a thundering herd. Some CDNs (CloudFront, Akamai) support both modes. The trade-off: origin push uses edge storage for content that may never be requested, while origin pull risks origin overload on first request for a hot URL — typically mitigated with request coalescing (the edge collapses N concurrent misses into 1 origin fetch).
**Visual:**
```
Origin pull (Cloudflare/Fastly/CloudFront):
  user -> edge -> (miss) -> origin -> cache + serve
  user -> edge -> (hit)  -> serve from cache
  Pros: adaptive, simple. Cons: thundering herd on cold hot URL.

Origin push (Netflix Open Connect):
  origin pre-positions content into edges during off-peak
  user -> edge -> (hit) -> serve from cache (origin never sees peak)
  Pros: handles massive concurrent demand. Cons: needs demand prediction.
```

### Q3. What is a cache key, and what are common mistakes in designing one?
**Answer:** The cache key is the unique identifier under which the CDN stores a cached response. The default is `{URL path} + {query string}`, but production CDNs let you customize it: include/exclude headers, ignore certain query params, normalize case, vary on `Accept-Encoding` for compression variants. Common mistakes: (1) **Including per-user data in the key** — e.g., including a `session_id` cookie in the key defeats caching entirely, because every user has a different session_id and you cache one entry per user. (2) **Ignoring meaningful headers** — if you ignore `Accept-Language` and serve the same cached response to all users, half your users get the wrong language. (3) **Including tracking params** — `?utm_source=email&utm_campaign=abc` produces a different cache key for every campaign, fragmenting your cache. Fix by excluding `utm_*` from the key. (4) **Not varying on `Accept-Encoding`** — if you cache only the gzip version and serve it to a client that requested brotli, you waste bandwidth. (5) **Case sensitivity** — `/Path` and `/path` are different keys in many CDNs; normalize to lowercase. (6) **Ignoring `Vary` headers** — the `Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language` response header tells the cache to store separate entries for each combination of those headers. The fix is to start with the default key, monitor your cache hit ratio, and tune carefully — a 95%+ hit ratio is the target for static content.
**Visual:**
```
Bad cache key (includes session_id):
  key = /api/user + cookie:session_id=abc123
  -> every user gets unique cache entry, 0% hit ratio

Good cache key (ignores session, includes meaningful vary):
  key = /api/products + Accept-Language + Accept-Encoding
  -> shared across users of same language/compression, high hit ratio

Cloudflare Cache Key rules:
  - include: path, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding
  - exclude: utm_*, session cookies, X-Request-ID
  - normalize: lowercase path, sort query params
```

### Q4. How does cache invalidation work, and what is stale-while-revalidate?
**Answer:** There are three invalidation strategies. (1) **TTL expiration** — the cached object has a `max-age` and is considered stale after that many seconds; the next request re-fetches from origin. Simple, but creates a "stale window" where users see outdated content for up to TTL seconds after a publish, and risks a thundering herd when the TTL expires and many concurrent requests hit origin simultaneously. (2) **Purge API** — when you publish new content, you call the CDN's purge API with the URL or a surrogate key (Fastly `Surrogate-Key`, Cloudflare `Cache-Tag`). Fastly's purge propagates in ~150 ms globally because it uses a messaging fabric; Cloudflare's takes ~30 seconds. (3) **Stale-while-revalidate (SWR)** — set `Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=60`. The CDN serves the cached object as fresh for 600 seconds. From 600–660 seconds, it serves the stale object to the user while asynchronously refreshing from origin in the background. After 660 seconds, it is fully expired and the next request is a synchronous origin fetch. SWR eliminates the thundering herd (because concurrent requests all get the same stale object while the background refresh happens once) and eliminates user-facing latency on refresh. The trade-off is that users may see content that is up to `max-age + stale-while-revalidate` seconds old. Netflix and YouTube use SWR heavily for episode metadata and thumbnails.
**Visual:**
```
Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=60

Timeline:
  T+0     -> cache filled from origin (fresh)
  T+0..600-> served as fresh (no origin hit)
  T+600   -> stale, but SWR window opens
  T+600..660 -> served stale + async refresh from origin (1 origin fetch)
  T+660+  -> expired, next request is synchronous origin fetch

Benefit: no thundering herd, no user-facing latency spike on refresh.
Trade-off: users may see content up to 660s old in worst case.
```

### Q5. What is edge compute and how does it differ from traditional CDN caching?
**Answer:** Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda@Edge, Fastly Compute@Edge) lets you run code at the CDN edge PoP, not just cache responses. Traditional CDN caching is passive: it can only return what origin returned, possibly transformed by simple rules (URL rewriting, header injection). Edge compute is active: you write a function that runs on every request, with full control over the request and response — you can route to different origins based on headers, do A/B testing at the edge, resize images on-demand, inject personalization, do bot mitigation, or even implement entire APIs that never touch origin. Cloudflare Workers run V8 isolates (not containers) in 300+ PoPs with sub-5ms cold starts. Lambda@Edge runs Node.js on CloudFront edges with ~50ms cold starts. Fastly Compute@Edge runs WebAssembly with sub-millisecond cold starts. The trade-offs: edge functions have strict CPU (Cloudflare: 50ms) and memory (128MB) limits, cannot easily maintain state across requests (you need a separate KV store like Cloudflare KV), and debugging is harder because the function runs at whichever PoP served the request. Netflix uses edge compute for A/B routing at the edge (which homepage variant does this user see?). Instagram uses it for image resizing — store one master image, resize at the edge for each requested dimension. The pattern is shifting more logic to the edge to reduce origin load and latency.
**Visual:**
```
Traditional CDN (passive cache):
  user -> edge -> (hit? serve cached : fetch from origin) -> user
  Edge can only return what origin returned (plus simple transforms).

Edge compute (active code at edge):
  user -> edge -> run Worker function (V8 isolate)
  Function can:
    - inspect request headers, cookies, geo
    - route to origin A or B based on A/B bucket
    - resize image, transform JSON, inject headers
    - return cached response if fresh, else fetch+cache
    - block bots, rate-limit, do auth at edge
  Origin never sees the request (for many use cases)
```

### Q6. How does Netflix's Open Connect CDN differ from a traditional CDN like Cloudflare?
**Answer:** Open Connect is Netflix's purpose-built CDN, optimized specifically for video delivery at extreme scale. Three key differences from a traditional CDN. (1) **Physical appliances inside ISPs** — Netflix ships free Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) into ISP datacenters worldwide, so the bytes flow from inside the user's ISP to the user without traversing the public internet backbone. This is "as close to the user as physically possible" — much closer than Cloudflare's PoPs, which are typically at internet exchange points. (2) **Origin push, not origin pull** — Netflix pre-positions content onto OCAs during off-peak hours based on predicted demand (release schedule, popularity models). When a new episode drops and 10 million users hit play simultaneously, the bytes are already local. Origin pull would melt the origin under that load. (3) **Purpose-built for video, not general web** — OCAs are optimized for large-file delivery with adaptive bitrate streaming over HTTP, not for low-latency API responses. Netflix does not need the dynamic, low-latency, edge-compute capabilities of Cloudflare; it needs massive sustained throughput for video. The trade-off: Open Connect only works for Netflix's content (it is a private CDN), while Cloudflare is multi-tenant. Netflix estimates Open Connect carries ~15% of global downstream internet traffic at peak — by far the largest single-application CDN in the world.
**Visual:**
```
Traditional CDN (Cloudflare):
  user -> ISP -> IXP -> Cloudflare PoP -> (miss) -> origin
                          (cache hit ratio ~95% for static)

Netflix Open Connect:
  user -> ISP -> OCA appliance (inside ISP datacenter)
                    (pre-positioned content, ~99% hit ratio)
                    origin never sees peak demand
  ~15% of global internet traffic flows this way
```

### Q7. How do CDNs handle HTTPS and TLS, and what are the trade-offs of edge termination?
**Answer:** CDNs terminate TLS at the edge — the user's TLS handshake completes against the edge PoP, not the origin. This means the CDN needs a certificate for your domain. Three options: (1) **Bring your own cert** — upload your cert to the CDN; the CDN terminates TLS and re-establishes a new TLS connection to origin (full end-to-end encryption, but you manage cert renewal). (2) **CDN-provided cert** — Cloudflare and others issue free Let's Encrypt certs automatically for your domain. (3) **Keyless SSL** — the CDN does the TLS handshake but signs the CertVerify with a key held in your HSM; the private key never leaves your infrastructure. Used by banks and regulated industries. Benefits of edge termination: TLS handshake CPU is offloaded from origin (significant at high request rates); the CDN can inspect and cache the response; TLS 1.3 0-RTT works at the edge for ultra-low latency. Trade-offs: (1) **Trust boundary** — if the CDN is compromised, the attacker can see decrypted traffic between user and edge. For sensitive data (banking, healthcare), this is unacceptable and you need end-to-end encryption (user -> edge -> origin all under TLS, with origin holding the private key). (2) **Certificate management** — the CDN needs valid certs for your domain; if renewal breaks, the entire site breaks. (3) **Mixed content** — if the CDN terminates TLS but origin serves HTTP, you have an unencrypted hop. The standard pattern is "TLS termination at edge + TLS to origin" (Cloudflare's "Full (strict)" mode), which gives you edge offload without an unencrypted hop.
**Visual:**
```
User --TLS-1.3--> Cloudflare edge --TLS--> origin
                 |                    |
                 terminates TLS       re-establishes TLS
                 (cert: edge)         (cert: origin)
                 CPU offloaded        origin sees plaintext (in TLS tunnel)

Keyless SSL (regulated industries):
  User --TLS--> edge --[transcript]--> customer HSM --[signature]--> edge
  Private key never leaves customer's HSM. Edge only signs the handshake.
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your e-commerce site has a global user base but origin in us-east-1. Users in Asia complain the site is slow. How do you use a CDN to fix it?
**Answer:** The bottleneck is almost certainly the 200 ms RTT between Asian users and the US-East origin, multiplied by the multiple round trips needed for TCP + TLS + HTTP. Layer three CDN optimizations. (1) **Static assets** — put your JS, CSS, images, fonts behind a CDN URL (e.g., `static.example.com`) with origin = your us-east-1 S3 bucket. Set `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` on versioned assets (file names include a hash like `app.abc123.js`). Use surrogate keys (`Cache-Tag: frontend`) for purging after deploys. Asian users now fetch these from a Singapore PoP in 5 ms instead of 200 ms. (2) **HTML pages** — set `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` so pages are cached at the edge for 60 seconds and refreshed in the background. (3) **TLS termination at edge** — let the CDN terminate TLS so the Asian user's TLS handshake completes against the Singapore PoP in 1 RTT (5 ms) instead of against origin (200 ms + 200 ms = 400 ms for TLS 1.3). For dynamic content that cannot be cached (e.g., cart, recommendations), use edge compute (Cloudflare Workers) to do personalization at the edge and only call origin for the actual cart mutation. Monitor your cache hit ratio — a 90%+ hit ratio means 90% of requests never touch origin, dropping origin load by 10x and Asian user TTFB from 800 ms to 100 ms.
**Visual:**
```
Before:                              After:
  user SG -> origin US-East            user SG -> SG CDN edge -> (hit) -> 5ms
  TCP: 200ms                           TLS handshake: 5ms (edge terminates)
  TLS: 400ms (2 RTT)                   static asset: 5ms (cache hit)
  HTML: 200ms                          HTML: 5ms (cached) + SWR refresh
  static asset: 200ms                  dynamic API: 5ms edge + 200ms origin
  total: ~1000ms TTFB                  total: ~100ms TTFB, origin load -10x
```

### Q2. A new product launch causes your origin to crash from a thundering herd of cache misses. How do you prevent this?
**Answer:** The thundering herd happens when a hot URL has no cache entry (just expired, just purged, or first-ever request) and thousands of concurrent users hit origin simultaneously because they all see the miss. Mitigations, in order of effectiveness. (1) **Request coalescing / request collapsing** — most CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront) will collapse N concurrent misses for the same URL into a single origin fetch; the other N-1 requests wait for the first to complete and then serve the cached result. Enable this. (2) **Stale-while-revalidate** — set `Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=60` so the CDN serves the stale entry for 60 seconds while refreshing in the background. This means the cache never blocks on origin synchronously after the first fill. (3) **Origin shield** — configure a single CDN PoP as a "shield" between all edges and origin. All edges fetch from the shield, which itself caches; the shield collapses concurrent origin requests to 1. Cloudflare's "Argo Tiered Caching" and Fastly's "Origin Shield" both do this. (4) **Pre-warm the cache** — before the launch, hit the URL from each region so the edges are populated. (5) **Graceful degradation at origin** — if origin does get overloaded, return a stale or simplified response (e.g., cached HTML without personalization) rather than 500ing. Netflix's API gateway returns degraded responses during thundering herds. (6) **Rate-limit at edge** — Cloudflare rate-limiting rules can cap the requests-per-second to origin per URL, queuing excess at the edge. The combination of origin shield + SWR + request coalescing eliminates 99% of thundering-herd incidents.
**Visual:**
```
Without mitigation:
  10k concurrent users -> all see cache miss -> 10k concurrent origin fetches
  -> origin CPU 100%, connection pool exhausted -> 500s -> cascade failure

With origin shield + SWR + coalescing:
  10k concurrent users -> edges check local cache
    miss -> edges fetch from shield (1 hop upstream)
    shield collapses 10k into 1 origin fetch
    edges serve stale-while-revalidate to waiting requests
  -> origin sees 1 request, returns 200, edges serve 10k from cache
```

### Q3. You publish a breaking news article that needs to be visible to all 1 billion users within 30 seconds. The CDN's global purge takes ~30 seconds. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** Two layers. (1) **Surrogate-key purge, not URL purge** — assign every article a surrogate key (`Cache-Tag: article-12345`) and purge by key, which is faster than URL-by-URL purging. Cloudflare's purge by Cache-Tag propagates in ~30 seconds globally; Fastly's instant purge propagates in ~150 ms via its messaging fabric. If you need sub-30-second, Fastly is the right choice. (2) **Versioned URLs for assets** — for the article's images and JS, use content-hashed URLs (`photo.abc123.jpg`) so you never need to purge them; you just publish a new URL when the asset changes. (3) **Short TTL with SWR on the HTML** — set `Cache-Control: max-age=10, stale-while-revalidate=30` on the article HTML. Users see the new content within 10 seconds (max-age) without a synchronous origin hit (SWR refreshes in background). (4) **Edge-side include (ESI) for the dynamic parts** — cache the article body for a long time, but include a tiny ESI fragment for the "breaking" badge that has a 0-second TTL. The edge assembles the page from cached body + fresh ESI fragment. (5) **Push-based invalidation** — for the most extreme cases, use a push-based cache invalidation system: when the article is published, your CMS calls every CDN region's purge API in parallel and waits for all to acknowledge before declaring the publish complete. (6) **Acceptable staleness** — if 30-second staleness is acceptable (which it usually is for a news article), do nothing special; the default purge is fine. The 30-second freshness requirement is unusual — for most content, a 5-minute SWR window is fine and far cheaper.
**Visual:**
```
Publishing pipeline:
  1. CMS publishes article-12345
  2. Push notification to purge service
  3. Purge service calls CDN API: POST /purge { Cache-Tag: "article-12345" }
  4. CDN evicts article-12345 across all PoPs (Fastly ~150ms, Cloudflare ~30s)
  5. Next request fills cache from origin

HTML caching strategy:
  Cache-Control: max-age=10, stale-while-revalidate=30
  -> users see new article within 10 seconds of publish
  -> no synchronous origin hit (SWR refreshes in background)
```

### Q4. Your CDN bill is $50k/month and growing. How do you reduce it?
**Answer:** Five levers. (1) **Increase cache hit ratio** — every cache hit is served from the edge (cheap); every miss is an origin fetch (expensive in origin CPU + egress). Audit your cache keys (exclude `utm_*` tracking params, ignore session cookies), set proper TTLs (1 year for versioned assets, 60s for HTML with SWR), and use origin shield to dedupe origin fetches. Going from 80% to 95% hit ratio cuts origin egress 3x. (2) **Negotiate committed-use discounts** — CDNs publish list prices ($0.085/GB for CloudFront) but offer 30–70% discounts for committed monthly volume. At $50k/month you have negotiating leverage; ask for a 50% discount for a 1-year commit. (3) **Tier your traffic** — not all bytes are equally important. Use a cheaper CDN (Bunny.net, KeyCDN) for static assets, and a premium CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai) only for dynamic/edge-compute traffic. Multi-CDN routing via DNS (Route 53 weighted) lets you shift traffic based on price. (4) **Compress more aggressively** — brotli compression is 15–25% smaller than gzip for text; PNG optimization (pngquant) cuts image bytes 50%. Less bytes = less bandwidth bill. (5) **Move large-file delivery to object storage with direct-to-S3 URLs** — for video, large PDFs, software downloads, use S3 presigned URLs directly (no CDN in the path) for low-traffic content; use CDN only for hot content. The S3 egress fee ($0.09/GB) is comparable to CDN, but you skip the CDN markup. Track your cost per GB served and per request as KPIs; Akamai and Cloudflare both offer cost analytics dashboards.
**Visual:**
```
Cost reduction levers:
  1. Hit ratio: 80% -> 95%   = origin egress -3x
  2. Negotiate: $0.085/GB -> $0.04/GB (committed use)  = -50%
  3. Tier traffic: hot on Cloudflare ($$$), tail on Bunny.net ($)
  4. Brotli + image optimization: bytes -20%
  5. S3 direct for large files: skip CDN markup on low-traffic content

Before: $50k/mo (list price, 80% hit, gzip only)
After:  ~$20k/mo (committed price, 95% hit, brotli, tiered)
```

### Q5. You need to serve different content to users in different countries (compliance, language, pricing). How do you use the CDN to do this?
**Answer:** Three patterns. (1) **Geolocation at the edge** — Cloudflare and CloudFront expose the user's country via the `CF-IPCountry` / `CloudFront-Viewer-Country` header. Your origin can read this header and return country-specific content. But you must include this header in the cache key (`Vary: CF-IPCountry` or Cloudflare Cache Key rules), otherwise the CDN will serve a German response to a French user. Trade-off: including country in the cache key multiplies your cache size by ~200 (number of countries), which can hurt hit ratio. (2) **Edge routing to country-specific origins** — use edge compute (Cloudflare Workers) to route `example.com` to `origin-de.example.com` for German users, `origin-fr.example.com` for French users. Each country has its own origin, and the edge routes based on the geo header. The cache key does not need to vary because the URL is the same but the upstream differs. (3) **Edge-side includes (ESI)** — cache the static shell of the page at the edge, and include dynamic country-specific fragments (price, language) as ESI includes with low TTL. The edge assembles the page from cached shell + fresh fragments, so most bytes are cached but the dynamic bits are fresh. Compliance-sensitive use case: GDPR requires EU users' data to stay in EU. Route EU users to an EU origin via the edge, never letting their requests touch US infrastructure. Cloudflare's Data Localization Suite enforces this at the edge.
**Visual:**
```
Pattern 1 (geo in cache key):
  user FR -> edge -> (cache key: /home + country=FR) -> origin returns French
  user DE -> edge -> (cache key: /home + country=DE) -> origin returns German
  Cache size: N x 200 countries. Risk: lower hit ratio.

Pattern 2 (edge routing):
  user FR -> edge Worker -> routes to origin-fr.example.com
  user DE -> edge Worker -> routes to origin-de.example.com
  Cache key: just /home. Each origin's content cached at edge.

Pattern 3 (ESI):
  user FR -> edge -> cached shell + ESI:price (FR) + ESI:lang (FR)
  Most bytes cached, only price/lang fragments are fresh per country.
```

### Q6. You are migrating from one CDN to another (Cloudflare to CloudFront). How do you do it with zero downtime?
**Answer:** The migration sequence. (1) **Configure CloudFront as a parallel CDN** — set up the same origin, the same cache behavior, the same TLS certs. CloudFront supports custom domains with ACM-managed certs. (2) **Test from a canary** — point a test hostname (`test-cdn.example.com`) at CloudFront and verify byte-for-byte identical responses vs the current Cloudflare setup. Diff headers, content-type, cache-control, status codes. (3) **Use DNS weighted routing for gradual cutover** — set up Route 53 weighted records: `cdn.example.com CNAME cloudflare-endpoint` (weight 95), `cdn.example.com CNAME cloudfront-endpoint` (weight 5). Monitor error rates, latency, cache hit ratio. If green, shift weights: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 95% -> 100% over a few days. (4) **Multi-CDN DNS** — for the migration period, use a DNS-based multi-CDN router (Cedexis, NS1, Route 53 weighted) that can fail over per-region: if CloudFront has higher error rate in Asia, route Asian traffic back to Cloudflare. (5) **Cache warming** — before flipping 100% to CloudFront, pre-warm its caches by replaying production traffic or hitting popular URLs from each region. A cold CloudFront edge will origin-storm your origin on cutover. (6) **Rollback plan** — keep the Cloudflare config live for 1 week after cutover so you can flip DNS back if CloudFront has issues. (7) **Purge coordination** — make sure your CMS purge logic calls both CDNs during the migration so cached content is consistent. The same multi-CDN pattern is useful in production for resilience (Cloudflare outage? Route to CloudFront via DNS in 60 seconds).
**Visual:**
```
T-0:   test-cdn.example.com -> CloudFront (canary, verify diffs vs Cloudflare)
T-1d:  cdn.example.com Route 53 weighted: 95% CF, 5% CloudFront
T-2d:  75% CF, 25% CloudFront  (monitor errors, latency, hit ratio)
T-3d:  50/50
T-4d:  25% CF, 75% CloudFront
T-5d:  5% CF, 95% CloudFront
T-7d:  100% CloudFront, Cloudflare config kept live for 1 week rollback
T-14d: decommission Cloudflare
```

### Q7. You serve user-uploaded images. Storing 10 pre-rendered sizes per image is expensive. How do you use a CDN to optimize this?
**Answer:** Store one master image on origin (S3) and resize on-demand at the CDN edge. Three implementations. (1) **Cloudflare Image Resizing** — request `https://images.example.com/photo.jpg?width=300&height=200` and Cloudflare's edge fetches the master, resizes, caches the result, and serves. The cache key includes the dimensions, so subsequent requests for the same size are hits. Storage cost drops 10x (one master instead of 10 sizes). (2) **Lambda@Edge for resizing** — write a Lambda function that runs at the CloudFront edge, fetches the master from S3, resizes with `sharp` or `libvips`, returns the resized image. CloudFront caches the response keyed on URL (which includes dimensions). Instagram uses a similar pattern for serving different image sizes. (3) **Fastly Compute@Edge with Wasm image libraries** — same idea, runs Wasm at the edge with sub-millisecond cold start. The trade-offs: edge resizing costs CPU (Cloudflare charges per resize, Lambda@Edge charges per invocation), so cache hit ratio matters — if you resize the same dimensions repeatedly, the cost amortizes. For very long-tail dimensions (one user requests a weird size), you may want to fall back to a pre-rendered set for popular sizes and use edge resize only for unusual ones. Also: edge resizing has a latency cost on first request (the resize itself takes 50–200 ms), but subsequent requests for the same size are served from cache in 5 ms. The pattern is "store one, transform on-demand, cache the result" — same pattern as Instagram, where the master is uploaded once and resized dynamically per device.
**Visual:**
```
Before (pre-rendered):
  origin stores: photo.jpg, photo-300x200.jpg, photo-600x400.jpg, ...
                 10 sizes per image, 10x storage cost

After (edge resize on-demand):
  origin stores: photo.jpg (master only)
  user requests: /photo.jpg?w=300&h=200
  edge: miss -> fetch master -> resize (50-200ms) -> cache + return
        hit  -> return from cache (5ms)
  Storage: 1x. Compute: per-resize cost, amortized by cache hits.
```

quiz.explanation: Origin pull is the default for web CDNs: the edge fetches content from origin on first request, caches it, and serves subsequent requests from cache until TTL expires. It is lazy — only content users actually request gets cached. This is appropriate for web assets (JS, CSS, images), API responses that are cacheable, and long-tail content where you cannot predict demand.

The default is {URL path} + {query string}, but production CDNs let you customize it: include/exclude headers, ignore certain query params, normalize case, vary on Accept-Encoding for compression variants.

quiz.explanation: There are three invalidation strategies. (1) TTL expiration — the cached object has a max-age and is considered stale after that many seconds; the next request re-fetches from origin. Simple, but creates a "stale window" where users see outdated content for up to TTL seconds after a publish, and risks a thundering herd when the TTL expires and many concurrent requests hit origin simultaneously.
